title: Explain the API Gateway pattern and its responsibilities.
shortTitle: The API Gateway pattern and its responsibilities
keyPoints: The API Gateway pattern puts one thin edge service in front of all services to own every cross-cutting concern.
Responsibilities include routing, protocol translation, authentication, aggregation, rate limiting, caching, observability, and resilience.
Each responsibility is a filter in an ordered chain; the request passes through each filter sequentially.
The gateway must never contain business logic, own data, or become a place for domain orchestration.
Protocol translation converts external REST/JSON to internal gRPC/protobuf without exposing internal protocols.
Backend-for-Frontend runs a tailored gateway per client type so mobile and web get different payloads.
In large systems, run multiple gateways or split into an edge gateway plus an internal service mesh.

s1_definition.oneliner: The API Gateway pattern puts one thin edge service in front of all your services to own every cross-cutting concern, and nothing that is business logic.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **API Gateway pattern** – a structural microservices pattern where a dedicated service acts as the single reverse-proxy entry point between external clients and internal services.
- **Responsibilities** – strictly cross-cutting: routing, protocol translation, authentication, aggregation, rate limiting, caching, observability (logging, tracing), and resilience (circuit breaking, retries).
- **Filter chain** – each responsibility is implemented as a filter in an ordered chain that the request passes through.
- **Boundary rule** – the gateway deliberately holds no business logic so it remains a thin, generic edge layer.
- **BFF variant** – Backend-for-Frontend runs a tailored gateway per client type (mobile, web, partner).
s1_definition.analogy: The API Gateway pattern is like having one official reception and security desk for the entire National Bank of India head office. Every visitor, whether Rajesh coming for a loan or Priya coming about her current account, enters through that one desk. The desk checks IDs, logs who came in and when, limits crowding, and sends each person to the right department. The desk never actually approves a loan or moves money; that is the department's job. It only manages access and direction.

```text
  API Gateway Pattern: Filter Chain
  ──────────────────────────────────
  Client Request
       │
       ▼
  ┌──────────────┐
  │ Tracing      │ → stamp traceId
  └──────┬───────┘
         ▼
  ┌──────────────┐
  │ Auth Filter  │ → validate JWT → reject 401 if invalid
  └──────┬───────┘
         ▼
  ┌──────────────┐
  │ Rate Limiter │ → check token bucket → reject 429 if exceeded
  └──────┬───────┘
         ▼
  ┌──────────────┐
  │ Router       │ → match path predicate → forward to service
  └──────┬───────┘
         ▼
  ┌──────────────┐
  │ Circuit Brkr │ → if service down → fallback
  └──────┬───────┘
         ▼
  Backend Service


  Backend-for-Frontend
  ────────────────────
  Mobile App ──▶ Mobile BFF Gateway (lean payload)
  Web App    ──▶ Web BFF Gateway (rich payload)
  Partner API ──▶ Partner Gateway (strict rate limits)
                      │
               ┌──────┼──────┐
           Account  Payment  Card
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The API Gateway pattern is a structural microservices pattern where one dedicated edge service becomes the single entry point between external clients and all the internal services. Its responsibilities are strictly cross-cutting: routing, protocol translation, authentication, aggregation, rate limiting, caching, observability, and resilience. The defining rule is that every one of those is a cross-cutting concern, and the gateway deliberately holds no business logic at all.

At National Bank of India, a request flows through an ordered chain of filters. The tracing filter stamps a correlation ID. The authentication filter verifies the JWT once at the edge. The rate-limit filter protects services from overload. The routing filter forwards the request to the right service. If any filter rejects the request, the chain stops immediately, so an unauthenticated call to the Payment Service is turned away at the edge and the service never sees it.

The gateway gives two big benefits: it decouples clients from the internal layout, because the app talks to one stable address while services behind it can change, and it removes duplicated edge logic, because authentication and rate limiting live in one place instead of being copied into every service. The discipline is to keep the gateway thin. It must not own business logic, data, or orchestration, because the moment it does, it becomes a distributed monolith.

Remember one sentence: the API Gateway pattern puts one thin edge service in front of all your services to own every cross-cutting concern, and nothing that is business logic.
